title: Problem Overview and History
content:
Erdős Problem #138 asks whether the van der Waerden numbers W(k) grow faster than any exponential function — specifically, whether W(k)^{1/k} → ∞ as k → ∞.

Van der Waerden proved in 1927 that W(k) is finite for all k: for any red-blue coloring of a sufficiently long string of integers, some k consecutive terms in arithmetic progression all have the same color. The number W(k) is the minimum length needed. The $500 prize reflects the difficulty: despite decades of work, the precise growth rate of W(k) remains a central open problem in Ramsey theory.
mathContext:
Known bounds:
- Lower: W(k) ≥ c · 2^k (Kozik–Shabanov 2016)
- Upper: W(k) ≤ 2^{2^{2^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}} (Gowers 2001)
- At primes: W(p+1) ≥ p · 2^p (Berlekamp 1968)

Exact values: W(3)=9, W(4)=35, W(5)=178, W(6)=1132

title: Monochromatic Arithmetic Progression
content:
A monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression is a sequence a, a+d, a+2d, ..., a+(k-1)d where all terms lie in {1,...,N} and all receive the same color. The common difference d must be positive to exclude degenerate single-point sequences.

Example: In a 2-coloring of {1,...,9}, the sequence 1, 4, 7 is a 3-term AP with d=3. Van der Waerden's theorem says any such coloring must have some 3-term AP with all terms the same color.

title: Coloring Definition
content:
A coloring of {1,...,N} using r colors assigns one of r colors to each integer in the range. This captures the Ramsey-theoretic setup for van der Waerden's theorem.

For the main problem we use r=2 (two colors, e.g. red/blue), but the definition works for any number of colors.
mathContext:
def ContainsMonoAPofLength {α} [AddCommMonoid α] {κ} [Finite κ] {M : Set α}
    (coloring : M → κ) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ c : κ, ∃ ap : Set M, Set.IsAPOfLength ((·.1) '' ap) k ∧ ∀ m ∈ ap, coloring m = c

A coloring is a function M → κ into a finite palette κ. For W(k) we take M = Finset.Icc 1 N (the interval {1,…,N}) and κ = Fin 2 (two colors). This predicate says the coloring contains a length-k monochromatic AP.
prerequisites: colorings of an interval (Finset.Icc) with Fin r

title: Guarantee Set and Its Nonemptiness
content:
The guarantee set GuaranteeSet(r,k) collects all N that are large enough: every r-coloring of {1,...,N} must contain a monochromatic k-AP. Van der Waerden's theorem says this set is nonempty for r,k ≥ 1.

The guarantee set is upward-closed: if N works, then N+1 also works (any coloring of {1,...,N+1} induces one on {1,...,N}). The van der Waerden number is the threshold — the minimum element.
prerequisites: the infimum sInf of a set
when a guarantee set is nonempty

title: Van der Waerden Number W(k)
content:
The van der Waerden number W(k) is the minimum N such that any 2-coloring of {1,...,N} contains a monochromatic k-term AP. It is defined as the infimum of the guarantee set for 2 colors and k terms.

The function is noncomputable: computing W(k) for given k requires searching exponentially many colorings, and for k ≥ 7 the exact value is unknown. The function is defined mathematically as a minimum but cannot be computed by a finite algorithm for arbitrary k.
mathContext:
noncomputable def monoAPNumber (r k : ℕ) : ℕ := sInf (monoAP_guarantee_set r k)
noncomputable abbrev W : ℕ → ℕ := monoAPNumber 2

Known values: W(3)=9, W(4)=35, W(5)=178, W(6)=1132. Beyond k=6, exact values are unknown.
prerequisites: van der Waerden's theorem (existence of W(k))

title: Van der Waerden's Theorem (Axiomatized)
content:
Van der Waerden's theorem (1927) is the bedrock: for any r colors and progression length k, there exists N large enough that every r-coloring of {1,...,N} contains a monochromatic k-term AP.

The proof uses double induction on (r, k). We axiomatize it here because formalizing the induction argument would require substantial additional infrastructure, while the theorem itself is well-established and not in doubt.
mathContext:
axiom W_is_nonempty (k : ℕ) : (monoAP_guarantee_set 2 k).Nonempty

Van der Waerden's theorem is recorded here in exactly the form needed to define W: the guarantee set for 2 colors and length k is nonempty. This makes W k = sInf (monoAP_guarantee_set 2 k) well-defined.

title: Berlekamp's Lower Bound (1968)
content:
Berlekamp proved that for prime p, W(p+1) ≥ p · 2^p. The construction colors integers {1,...,p·2^p} by writing each integer n as n = a · 2^b mod p (roughly), using the structure of GF(p) × Z/2Z. This coloring avoids any monochromatic (p+1)-term AP.

This gives strong bounds at prime values: W(3) ≥ 8, W(4) ≥ 24, W(6) ≥ 160. The actual values W(3)=9, W(4)=35, W(6)=1132 show Berlekamp's bound is often quite close at p=2,3 but loose for larger primes.
mathContext:
axiom berlekamp_lower_bound (p : ℕ) (_hp : p.Prime) :
  p * 2 ^ p ≤ W (p + 1)

Sample bounds:
- p=2: W(3) ≥ 8  (actual: W(3) = 9)  ← tight!
- p=3: W(4) ≥ 24 (actual: W(4) = 35)
- p=5: W(6) ≥ 160 (actual: W(6) = 1132)
prerequisites: finite fields GF(p) and discrete logarithms

title: Gowers' Upper Bound (2001)
content:
Gowers proved the best known upper bound: W(k) ≤ 2^{2^{2^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}}, a tower of five exponentials. This follows from his analytic proof of Szemerédi's theorem using Gowers uniformity norms.

Earlier upper bounds used Ackermann-type functions (van der Waerden 1927) or primitive recursive but still enormous bounds (Shelah 1988). Gowers' breakthrough was the first elementary tower bound. He received a Fields Medal partly for this work.
mathContext:
axiom gowers_upper_bound (k : ℕ) :
  W k ≤ 2 ^ (2 ^ (2 ^ (2 ^ (2 ^ (k + 9)))))

Even for k=3 this gives an astronomically large bound, dwarfing the true value W(3)=9.

title: Kozik–Shabanov Lower Bound (2016)
content:
Kozik and Shabanov proved the best known general lower bound: W(k) ≥ c · 2^k for some absolute constant c > 0, valid for all k ≥ 1. The proof uses the Lovász Local Lemma to show that a random coloring, after suitable conditioning, avoids long monochromatic APs.

This tells us W(k) is at least exponential. But the main conjecture asks whether W(k) grows faster than ANY exponential, i.e., super-exponentially.
mathContext:
axiom kozik_shabanov_lower_bound :
  ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → c * 2 ^ k ≤ (W k : ℝ)

Contrast: this says W(k)/2^k ≥ c (bounded below), while ExponentialDiverges asks W(k)/2^k → ∞.

title: Exact Small Values
content:
Exact values of W(k) are known for k ≤ 6:
- W(3) = 9: proved by elementary arguments
- W(4) = 35: verified by exhaustive search
- W(5) = 178: computed by Landman and Robertson (2014)
- W(6) = 1132: computed by Kouril and Paul (2008) using SAT solvers

The growth ratios 3.9×, 5.1×, 6.4× suggest acceleration consistent with the conjecture. Beyond k=6, exact values are unknown — the computation is believed to be intractable.
mathContext:
axiom W_three : W 3 = 9
axiom W_four  : W 4 = 35
axiom W_five  : W 5 = 178
axiom W_six   : W 6 = 1132

Growth ratios: W(4)/W(3) ≈ 3.9, W(5)/W(4) ≈ 5.1, W(6)/W(5) ≈ 6.4

title: Erdős Problem #138 — Main Conjecture
content:
The main open question: does W(k)^{1/k} → ∞? This asks whether van der Waerden numbers grow faster than any exponential. For any constant base c > 0 (no matter how large), eventually W(k) > c^k.

The Kozik–Shabanov bound shows W(k) ≥ c_0 · 2^k (so W(k)^{1/k} ≥ c_0^{1/k} · 2), which tends to 2 — not to infinity. The gap between the known exponential lower bound and the conjecture's super-exponential claim is the heart of the open problem.
mathContext:
def Erdos138Conjecture : Prop :=
  Tendsto (fun k => (W k : ℝ) ^ ((k : ℝ)⁻¹)) atTop atTop

Filter.Tendsto f atTop atTop means: for every M > 0, eventually f(k) > M.
Here f(k) = W(k)^{1/k}, the k-th root of W(k).

title: Related Questions from Erdős (1980–1981)
content:
Erdős posed several related questions about how rapidly W(k) grows:

1. **QuotientDiverges**: Does W(k+1)/W(k) → ∞? (Consecutive van der Waerden numbers have unbounded ratio)
2. **DifferenceDiverges**: Does W(k+1) − W(k) → ∞? (Consecutive gaps grow unboundedly)
3. **ExponentialDiverges**: Does W(k)/2^k → ∞? (Growth faster than 2^k)

QuotientDiverges and ExponentialDiverges remain open. DifferenceDiverges is now RESOLVED affirmatively (DeepMind AlphaProof Nexus, 2026-05-21): the unconditional bound W(k+1) − W(k) ≥ k gives W(k+1) − W(k) → ∞. The main conjecture (W(k)^{1/k} → ∞) implies ExponentialDiverges.

title: Implication Chain: Main Conjecture → ExponentialDiverges
content:
The main conjecture implies ExponentialDiverges: if W(k)^{1/k} → ∞, then for any M > 0, eventually W(k)^{1/k} > M, so W(k) > M^k. Taking M > 2 gives W(k) > 2^k · (M/2)^k → ∞, hence W(k)/2^k → ∞.

This shows the main conjecture is strictly stronger than ExponentialDiverges. The sorry in the Lean proof marks that formalizing this limit argument (using Mathlib's filter machinery) is incomplete, though the mathematics is clear.
mathContext:
theorem main_conjecture_implies_exponential :
    Erdos138Conjecture → ExponentialDiverges := by
  intro _hconj
  sorry  -- Requires filter composition and rpow/pow monotonicity

The logical chain:
  W(k)^{1/k} → ∞  ⟹  W(k)/2^k → ∞  (by comparing k-th roots)
